records.title: Show HN: PewPewPew – Multiplayer Asteroids with deterministic rollback at 60hz
records.author: Benjaminsen
records.storyText:
I have been building realtime multiplayer games that run in a browser since 1999 and my latest is pewpewpew.io which combines everything I know about doing this well.

The game uses a fully client and server synchronized state machine running at 60hz with rollback / rollforward on both client and server.

During normal play only user input is transmitted using a compressed message format, where input is 7 fields in 2 bytes, with a total of about 26KB/s used for a room with 32 active players.

Users are automatically distributed into a room on a server with the lowest measured ping where there are other players playing.

Currently running using cloudflare Durable Objects, but I expect to offload it to dedicated metal should the cost go above $500 / month. Current monthly cost sits at about $300 per 1K average CCU.

Works on mobile, free to play, no ads, no signup.

P.S. Unlike some of our competition we do not use relays like AWS SES. In fact mxRaven was born from the open source raven library (https://github.com/synqronlabs/raven) a high performance comprehensive ESMTP toolkit I wrote in Go. We ARE the email relay, and even the core transport and email auth library is first party and open source, something I am very proud of.

records.title: Show HN: 2D world SIM where each creature runs a text classifier in the browser
records.author: nico
records.storyText:
Each creature in this data lab is a real text classifier. You put together a workflow, and the creatures execute it. Just set a stream of incoming messages and watch them work: one filters out the spam, another tags each message's mood, finally a router sends each message to the right bin, and anything it isn't sure about goes to review

The classifiers run entirely in your browser. It uses a 22.7M parameter model, int8 ONNX, about 10 ms a message, no API calls

Outside the lab, the creatures also evolve, chat, gossip, build huts, plot charts, count numbers, process and eat words, code and dream when asleep. You can also see their stream of consciousness, which they turn into thoughts that they tag. And when they are asleep, you can watch their dreams

There are a lot of ways of modifying or evolving the environment and the creatures, including adding elements from other websites, playing music and changing the weather

And if you want to change anything at all, talk to the Operator (or make it smarter), connect it to your Claude or OpenAI subscription, or setup your API key, or point it to a local model in Ollama or LM Studio, and you can edit the whole world via chat, without limits (get the code here: https://github.com/nicobrenner/id-le)

What else would you like the creatures to do?

PS: Happy Halloween

records.title: Show HN: Nomos – A Go harness that stops coding agents from cheating on tests
records.author: mgantlett
records.storyText:
Hi HN, Mark here.

If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you.

Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up.

Starting over the summer I built Nomos: a single 28MB stripped static Go binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, Apache 2.0) that sits between your repo and whatever coding agent you already use. You run "nomos init" once and keep prompting in plain English - the agent drives the worktree, verification, and self-fix loop under the hood.

Instead of trusting prompts, Nomos locks main read-only via Git hooks, separates spec/contract tasks (INT-) from code tasks (SUB-) in a local causal DAG (nomos task dag) so an agent can't edit the spec to excuse broken code, and isolates every task in a Git worktree (worktrees/<repo>-<task>) under a strict state machine (IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN). Throwing away a bad run is free.

Before anything merges to main, "nomos verify" runs 42 in-binary structural/AST gates (~460ms full pass, ~24ms single-file via --fast-file) plus your repo's own compiler and test suite. It blocks fake shims, deleted assertions, skipped tests (t.Skip, @pytest.mark.skip, #[ignore], @Disabled, [Fact(Skip=...)]), leaked secrets, functions over 60 LOC, complexity spikes, hardcoded paths, symlinks, and nomos.yaml rubric tampering against pinned main, returning file:line fixes for the next turn. Any gate failure or panic aborts the two-phase merge before main moves.

"nomos mem" stores architectural lessons locally in embedded pure-Go SQLite (mneme.db), promoting patterns only after a verified merge with a Git Notes receipt (refs/notes/nomos/releases) so failed runs don't poison memory. No cloud account, daemon, or telemetry.

One fun lesson from running the PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks against the public TraceTrial-Bench harness benchmark (arXiv:2610.32285 - summary and spec in the repo README): my first PostToolUse hook injected helpful "process failure / refusal" warnings into tool results, and it degraded native OS EACCES guardrail attribution by -39.3% because synthetic hook text polluted error channels. Compiling "nomos hook" (session-start, pre-tool, post-tool at ~4ms cold start), keeping PostToolUse silent on native channels, and moving enforcement to PreToolUse path guards plus a 3-strike identical-failure circuit-breaker recovered that -39.3% drop and lifted stateful handoff, context continuity, and guardrail tasks cleanly.

Two rough edges upfront. First, while full type-checking, tests, and coverage ratchets (go test, LCOV, Cobertura XML) run via native toolchains across Go, TS/Svelte, Python, Rust, C/C++, Java/Kotlin, and C#, the fast in-binary pass uses go/ast for Go and combines a wazero WASM linear-memory cache and .scm query compiler with pure-Go multiline lexical scanners rather than bundling multi-MB per-language .wasm grammars (keeping the binary 28MB, CGO_ENABLED=0). Second, running the full IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN loop adds turn overhead, so for a 100-line weekend prototype raw vibe-coding is faster - Nomos is for repos you still have to understand six months from now.

Curious how others here fence coding agents in on real repos (containers, Git hooks, jj workspaces, custom linters?), and what sneakier "make the build green" shortcuts still slip past your checks.

records.title: Show HN: AWKLog – a minimalist Datalog interpreter in Awk
records.author: stass
records.storyText:
For many of the projects I work on I found myself wanting to use a relational language like Datalog to generate C source from specifications, do verification during build or maintain a task database.

However pulling a full blown Souffle or SWI-PL as a build dependency is always a PITA and also an overkill.

So I (with the help of Claude) built awklog, a pure POSIX awk based interpreter. Copy it to your project and use during build stage or test stage with no extra dependencies.

It's a semi-naive interpreter, so decently fast, and certainly fast enough for anything you might need to do as a dev tool.

One cool usecase in particular I've been a heavy user of is a task system maintained directly in the project git repo. Just create a text file with tuples describing your tasks, their states, dependencies, hypotheses and so on. AWKLog will be able to query it for you, even recursively, and provide instant answers. Easy for AI agents to query too and no remote infrastructure dependencies at all. Everything stays in GIT, version controlled.

I hope other people will find this tool useful too.

records.title: Show HN: People you know, an end-to-end encrypted private Instagram replacement
records.author: jsbg
records.storyText:
I built an alternative to popular social networks because I was sick of the unending enshittification of instagram. Every UX change in recent years intended to make their app more addictive to teenagers has made me want to use it less, but I don't want to lose contact with the actual people that are close to me. First it was stories to make it your job to open the app every day, and then "everything is a reel" to try to get you to scroll infinitely.

This app is a more minimalist way to share photos and short videos with people you actually know. There are no public profiles so no follows, only mutuals. The feed is in reverse chronological order and there are no suggested posts or suggested connections. When sharing, you can choose the audience (you can create groups or select individual people), it's not necessarily to all your mutuals.

Other UX niceties I added are the fact that you can only see comments on your friends' posts from people you know (so no more terrible takes from their random uncle you've never met). There is also the concept of albums where the audience is the album members, who are not necessarily connected to each other, which can be useful for events or group trips.

Beyond the worsening UX of other apps, I know a lot of people who have left social media, either by deleting their account or by just never interacting, because they don't trust big tech companies with their media. E.g. people who don't share photos of their family on facebook even to only their friends. The end-to-end encryption part of the app is there for those people as well. What you share is encrypted with post-quantum keys and only the people you share a post with have the keys to decrypt it on their phone. Someone with access to the database cannot see media, captions, comments, display names, profile photos, and album and group names.

The app will never show ads since I believe that that's what drives a lot of the UX decisions on the other platforms.

It's available on both android and ios currently in Singapore, Japan, New Zealand, USA, and Canada, because those had a relatively low barrier to entry, but if there is interest I will add other countries eventually. In particular, EU countries require a legal representative there that it doesn't make sense for me to pay for right now.

records.title: Show HN: CheckOwners to find your repo's hidden single points of failure
records.author: smusali
records.storyText:
Hey HN Community!

I created checkOwners to solve a problem by many engineering teams: who knows your codebase, and what will happen when they go away?

This is an open-source, local-first tool which performs analysis based on Git history in order to find hidden knowledge risk in repositories.

It is able to recognize true experts, recognize out-of-date ownership definitions, find knowledge bottlenecks, propose review candidates, and model what would happen when contributors go away.

All the magic happens on your own local system without uploading source code or an LLM. It also works within GitHub Actions.

Try it: ``` pip install checkowners checkowners audit checkowners risk ```

Would appreciate any feedback from maintainers and platform engineers regarding the accuracy of Git history reflection of expertise and findings of risk analysis.

records.title: Show HN: A faster Python 3 interpreter implemented in C11, one week
records.author: soasme
records.storyText:
Small Python (spy) is a small, embeddable Python engine written in C11. Pretty much like quickjs for javascript, it's for Python.

The entire Python core language features is full implemented with almost all builtins. No Lib/ is included except sys/gc that changes the interpreter behaviors.

Is missing Python stdlib a pain? Probably no. Host injected modules allows any language's ecosystem to be used in Python syntax. Check examples, you can build game by using Raylib, or build web server using Axum/Serde_python (using Rust crates).

Just copy `spy.h`, `spyc-*.c` into your project and use it as a C library. Or several bindings are provided for languages like Js, Python, Rust, Go. You can install via pip, npm, crate, go. Worker mode is recommended so that any issue would be contained in a subprocess.

It's fast. Well, not at the speed of Pypy because it's not JIT. But it's slightly faster than C Python in most benched cases.

Another good feature is compiling Python into a binary. You could use PyInstaller, but it's gonna be so large. Small Python's binary is small. A raylib + spy based PONG game is built at around 2MB.

It's using a full suite of tests: unittest, fuzz, sanitize, bench, TLA+ specs. Despite using C, agents are unable to spot a single segfault as of now. So that's pretty cool. :)

The roadmap aims to build it for agents: snapshot/resume between durable sessions, policy declaration so agents never shoot on your feet, etc.

It has been built for one week. I have a long Claude Code session running over several days with /remote-control using Opus 5.5.

Repo url: https://github.com/soasme/small-python Previous HN post: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50281226

records.title: Show HN: Gradual Daylight Saving – Spread the 1-hour shifts over the whole year
records.author: johndimm
records.storyText:
Instead of jumping an hour twice a year, shift a little bit each day. The offset rises smoothly from 0 at winter solstice to +60 minutes at summer solstice and back. Max daily change is ~32 seconds.

William Willett's original 1907 proposal was actually 8 shifts of 20 minutes —- four forward in spring, four back in autumn. Gentler on humans than what we ended up with. Now that most clocks are networked, there's no reason to stop at 8.

The site has an interactive demo with two clocks (official vs. smooth), a year-long offset chart, and a working Smooth Time clock you can use as an alarm. Built with Next.js.

records.title: Show HN: Slop Node for Keeta
records.author: xescure
records.storyText:
...the first publicly available node software for Keeta. Created with heavy use of AI agents. Not affiliated with Keeta.

You can run a replica, a peering node or a (testnet) rep with Docker in a few lines. Mine is running at https://node.xescu.re/api/node/version

The true digitalization of finance, especially in cross-border contexts, has stalled. Blockchain technology may bring about a new chapter where money is as fast as the internet is. However, current blockchains are unscalable and clunky and I don't see them being the next financial backbone at all.

Keeta is insanely fast. (Google measured 11 million transactions per second: https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/financial-services/how-...) Settlement is sub-second and deterministic. Keeta's mental model maps cleanly to payments, and it doesn't try to force smart contracts where they're not needed. Tokens can be equipped with KYC/AML/sanctions controls for assets and jurisdictions that so require. Ramps, bridges, and liquidity providers are not an afterthought, but native first-class participants of the network. Using these components, for the first time in history, a solo developer with an AI agent can set up an entire neobank in just minutes. I believe Keeta will power a new wave of financial apps, where the best user experience, security, and feature set will win. Builders can focus on building, and the open and interoperable network takes care of providing them with the best infrastructure, instead of depending on closed-room financial deals.

I can't wait to see how Keeta develops, but right now its source code isn't fully public and third parties are not able to run their own nodes. I fed Claude Opus 5.5 the public parts of the code, my understanding of Keeta, its docs and forum discussions. Then came about 6 hours of refinement and setting up an environment where the agent could evaluate itself. Finally, it ran for a few days autonomously:

The end result is a fully functional Keeta node. It's primarily for experimentation, please don't rely on it for high value applications (yet?).

records.title: Show HN: EchoChain to see what happens when LLMs play telephone
records.author: smusali
records.storyText:
Hey HN Community!

I created `echoChain` to explore the following phenomenon: how much data retained after LLMs exchange responses multiple times?

Imagine the game of telephone but with AIs. Each model converts the response into a question, which is then answered. After several rounds, facts get mutated, details get stripped, and the answer is far removed from the initial one.

`echoChain` is an OSS Python CLI that helps measure this process. It allows for multi-model testing, model rotation, tracking of factual claims, semantic similarity calculations, fidelity scores, reproducibility, statical tests, and visualizations. You can test models against each other, try various configurations, and learn which ones retain the most information. Right now, it only support OpenRouter; so, for this reason, please, make sure you set `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` before running it.

I wonder about the implications of these results for multi-agent systems, where AI-created information flows between agents without any human validation.

Looking forward to hearing your feedback on LLM agent building and evaluation frameworks!

records.title: Show HN: Corollary, LaTeX Editor for Mac with On-Device Apple Foundation Models
records.author: calvinyz
records.storyText:
A few days ago, I got OpenAI's email that Prism will be officially shutting down on January 1. Having written my last paper in it, I was quite disappointed since I've never really enjoyed typing LaTeX by hand for long periods. Also, when I updated my macOS recently, I started playing around with Apple's Foundation Models a bit (which I'm late on). So on Saturday I decided that, instead of studying for my midterms, my weekend project was going to be building a local version of Prism that used on-device Apple FMs.

It's an Overleaf-style editor with a PDF preview that compiles with TeX Live, and it installs TeX for you if you don't have it. To use the AI features, select text and press Cmd-K, and you can accept or reject the diff. If you have a handwritten formula that you want to insert, you can place your cursor where you want to insert and drop in a photo, which GLM-OCR turns into LaTeX locally since Apple's OCR doesn't handle math.

What was fun was testing out the capability of the models. Corollary uses SystemLanguageModel.default, which is Apple's general-purpose on-device model and the one built into macOS for Apple Intelligence. It's about 3B params with a 4,096 token context window on my M1 Max. When asked for plain text, it kept every \cite, \ref, \label and formula intact in 78 of 80 edits, but with structured output (@Generable) it went 0 for 20 because the JSON escaping eats the backslashes (\text comes back as a tab). While this limits capabilities like full document edits, you can already point it at Ollama or your own API key, and I'm sure the models will catch up soon.

Also, it needs an Apple silicon Mac, and the AI needs macOS 26 with Apple Intelligence. At this stage I don't have an Apple Developer ID yet, so the first launch needs System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway. Sorry about that. Please give it a try and let me know what bugs you run into or what the model struggles on!

Github: https://github.com/calvinyz/corollary

records.title: Show HN: Nonce – Open-source, least-privilege Gmail access for AI agents
records.author: richardmeng
records.storyText:
Hi HN! We built nonce, an open-source tool that sits between personal AI agents (Muse, Grok, ChatGPT, Claude) and your personal data in Gmail, Calendar, Drive and more.

Today, if you connect Gmail to an AI agent like Muse, it can read your entire inbox. Whether on purpose or not, they can read far more emails than needed. This poses a huge data-privilege risk, in which personal data is accessed without limits.

With nonce, the AI will no longer hold your Google or Slack tokens. To read anything, it has to show its intent first:

User's question: When does my flight to Tokyo leave? Agent's justification: Need the airline confirmation email Agent's search query: from:united.com Tokyo Access needed: 10 minutes

If the justification and search query are reasonable, nonce issues a scoped token to the AI Agent. AI Agent can only query data using a token.

If something looks fishy, i.e the AI is acting on its own, wants too much, or wants sensitive emails like bank statements, medical results, or password resets. nonce sends you a notification to approve or deny.

By default, nonce denies massive crawling behaviors

How it works 1. nonce scores each search against your original question before running it, to ensure its relevance. 2. Every search is combined with the token's search. If the AI searches "bank statement", nonce runs (from:united.com Tokyo) AND (bank statement). It can narrow its access, but not widen it. 3. The token is scoped to that agent only, with a TTL for X minutes.

Limitations: nonce can't see your chat with the AI, so it can't prove you asked, which leaves a risk that the AI Agent can fake the intent. However, users can audit past accesses in nonce portal and identify these bypasses.

Give it a shot at https://github.com/roe-ai/nonce We'd love to hear what you think.

Website: https://anonce.io

records.title: Show HN: Devpush – Self-Hosted PaaS for Docker Compose
records.author: hunvreus
records.storyText:
I wanted Vercel-style deploys on my own VPS. That's devpush.

I released the first version last year as a Vercel clone for Python apps [1]. It worked, but I couldn't keep up with feature requests, because every new stack needed its own Docker image. I also wanted it to manage multiple servers and be easier to install.

So I rewrote it as a much lighter Docker Compose PaaS. You can deploy it on Cloudflare for free and connect as many VPS as you want. Some of the stuff I think is cool:

- No SSH access to your servers required. - Works with any Docker Compose setup. - Backups and restores for volumes and databases. - Git-based deploys and rollbacks. - API and MCP. - Free and open source (MIT).

The code is at https://github.com/hunvreus/devpush

You can also kick the tires, using the free trial of the hosted version: https://app.devpu.sh/

[1]: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45501279

records.title: Show HN: Mistake Trainer – Spaced repetition from your own Lichess games
records.author: pandigital
records.storyText:
I’m an 1800 player on Lichess and struggle making the same types of mistakes over and over again. Lichess has a nice feature called “Learn from your mistakes” available after you request a computer analysis. I wanted something a little more so I built Mistake Trainer with Claude Code.

It expands “Learn from your mistakes” to all your computer analyzed games and adds spaced repetition with the UI ported from lila so it feels like y̶o̶u̶’̶r̶e̶ b̶a̶t̶m̶a̶n̶ playing on Lichess. If you don’t play on Lichess, or don’t want to use your own account at first, there is a sample deck included so you can check it out.

There is also the option to use your own computer analysis to create cards from all of your Lichess games, not just the ones analyzed on Lichess’s servers. If you have lots of games, I recommend using your own computer to download the app so you have access to a better engine.

Other features included: suspending cards (positions) you don’t like, choosing if you want to focus on opening mistakes vs mistakes where your position collapsed, toggling your previous move arrow (this was a nitpicky one for me). Crucially, you can adjust how long a delay before you see a card again. I found somewhere between a 5 to 7 day delay was helpful to prevent just superficially recognizing a solution.

Similar tools that already exist include Aimchess and github.com/antimike/chess_trainer. I have the greatest respect for Lichess, and tried to build a tool that feels like a natural extension of their wonderful service.

Mistake Trainer is free, open source, and has no server to see your data (it stays on your computer). I hope you find it helpful in improving your chess!

https://github.com/DannyNagelMath/Mistake-Trainer

records.title: Show HN: Crosswalk – terminal manager to reduce sprawl
records.author: josephspurrier
records.storyText:
I usually have many projects and terminals I’m working in so Crosswalk groups my work together and allows me to open a terminal (or another terminal app) in the correct folder/project quickly and label the tab (as well as add notes). I started on iTerm2 (which is great) years ago for my terminal manager, then found I spent too much time flipping between tabs once I started leveraging terminal agents like Claude Code and Codex so I built Crosswalk to improve visibility at a glance. It originally started as a web page, but then I moved it to an app so I had better control over notifications and sounds to let me know when work was done or needed me on one of the tabs.

Crosswalk shows which sessions are still working or sitting idle with an activity dot on the tab. It provides hotkeys to jump between tabs and groups quickly. Even if you're not using agents, you can still use it for your terminal work - I commonly leave active projects as groups on the left even if I not working in them right now. There's an MCP server so an agent can launch new tabs (and agents) - it's helpful when you need a lead agent to spawn long running agents (in visible tabs) and then monitor their status (running, stuck, needs user feedback) or compact their context at efficient times. There are other nice features like layouts to view multiple terminals at once and reopens terminals from last session. I spent a bunch of time iterating on the pty host (pseudoterminal host) so updating the app or closing and then reopening will restore the sessions.

This is a paid product you can trial for free. I created it to solve the multi agent bottlenecks so I use it daily, both personally and professionally. For Mac and Windows - Electron based.

records.title: Show HN: DSP Explorables
records.author: FLT8
records.storyText:
I spent the weekend with Claude assembling some pages for interactive exploration of a variety of basic DSP topics.

I have published the pages at https://dsp.gundy.dev/

My main goal, initially, was to build something for myself, as a way to refresh my memory and/or satisfy my curiosity on topics I love. My problem is that I find signal processing textbooks dry. Static diagrams and heavy math don't engage me very well, and I much prefer things I can interact with. As the pages started taking shape, I started thinking others might get some benefit too.

I've tried to keep the pages relatively light on math, except where it genuinely illuminates, and also keep the pages full of interactive examples. For example an in-browser acoustic modem is built up piece-by-piece and used to demonstrate modulation; multiple synths are playable with MIDI keyboards; many pages give you the ability to record your own samples and use them eg. for pitch shifting or compression or modelling your own guitar body in the physical modelling page. There's the ability to measure the SNR of your own room to determine its capacity to carry information, and much more.

I'm genuinely interested in any and all feedback - things that I could have covered better, other topics to include etc. I still have a roadmap of a number of things I'd like to cover, and I figured before I get too much deeper, it could benefit from some wider socialisation and feedback.

Also note: this is an ad-free hobby project and for the foreseeable future will remain that way.

All demos run in the browser only, no data is sent to, or processed by anything other than your own machine.

Thanks!

records.title: Show HN: LAN Commander – Native C++ TUI File Manager for Windows (700 KB)
records.author: SoftDevelopUA
records.storyText:
Hi HN! I’m an independent developer from Ukraine, and I missed the simplicity and raw speed of classic dual-panel tools like Far Manager and Norton Commander.

I built LAN Commander — a modern, keyboard-driven TUI file manager written in native C++ for Windows: - 100% portable, single binary under 1 MB (~700 KB) with zero dependencies. - Non-blocking asynchronous background file operations and drive monitoring. - Built-in multi-threaded LAN scanner (SMB/NetBIOS ports 445/139). - Integrated text & Hex editor with syntax highlighting and regex search. - Full support for smooth scrolling, VFS, and even a built-in classic Tetris.

It is available here: https://softdevelop-ua.itch.io/lan-commander

I would love to get your thoughts, architectural feedback, and feature suggestions!
